questions.question: A table in Ms. Lee's class lists the masses, in kilograms, of 5 backpacks. The five numbers in the table are 4, 5, 5, 6, and 30, and the 30 kg backpack holds a set of textbooks. Which measure best describes a typical backpack mass in this table?
options: The median, because 30 kg pulls the mean far up
The mean, because the mean is always the best one
The mode, because 30 kg pulls the median far up
The mean, because it uses every value in the table
questions.explain: One value far from the rest (30 kg) drags the mean toward itself, so the median is the fairer summary here. The common trap is choosing the mean just because it uses every number, or blaming the median for the shift.

questions.question: A table at the school store lists the size of each of the 7 T-shirts sold this week. The seven entries in the table are S, M, M, M, L, L, and XL. Which measure best describes the size that a typical customer bought?
options: The mean, found by adding sizes and dividing by 7
The mode, since the sizes are words, not numbers
None of them, since sizes cannot be summarized
The mean, because it uses every shirt that sold
questions.explain: Sizes are categories, not numbers, so you cannot add or order-and-halve them; the mode, M, is the only measure that works. The trap is reaching for the mean out of habit when the data is not numerical.

questions.question: A table lists the number of minutes 5 students practised piano on Sunday. The five values in the table are 20, 25, 30, 35, and 150, where 150 belongs to a student preparing for an exam. Which statement about that 150 is true?
options: The 150 raises the median far more than the mean
The 150 changes the median but leaves the mean
The 150 lifts the mean far more than the median
The 150 changes neither the mean nor the median
questions.explain: The mean adds every value, so 150 pushes it to 52, while the median only slides to the middle value, 30. The trap is thinking an extreme value moves the median most; the median barely notices it.

questions.question: A table lists the price, in dollars, of each of the 6 hoodies a school sells. The six prices in the table are 30, 32, 34, 35, 36, and 95, where 95 is a limited edition hoodie. The mean of the table is $43.67 and the median is $34.50. Which sentence best explains why these two numbers are so far apart?
options: The $95 pulled the median above the mean value
The median is low because it ignores the $30 price
The mean is higher because it is the best measure
The $95 pulled the mean above most of the prices
questions.explain: Adding $95 into the total lifts the mean above five of the six prices, while the median stays between $34 and $35. The trap is assuming the higher number must be the better description of a typical hoodie.

questions.question: The data set 6, 7, 8, 9, 10 has a mean of 8 and a median of 8. The value 40 is now added to the set. Which statement correctly describes what happens to the two measures?
options: The mean rises to 13.33; the median only to 8.5
Both rise to 13.33, since 40 counts in each
The median rises to 13.33; the mean only to 8.5
The median jumps to 20; the mean barely moves
questions.explain: The new total is 80 over 6 values, so the mean jumps to about 13.33, while the median is just the average of the two middle values, 8 and 9, giving 8.5. The trap is expecting 40 to drag the median along with it.

questions.question: Ten houses on a Surrey street sold last year. Nine of them sold for between $700 000 and $900 000, and one sold for $4 million. A news report wants a single number for the typical selling price on that street. Which choice is best?
options: The mean, since it uses all ten selling prices
The median, since the $4 million skews the mean
The mode, since the median is skewed the most
The mean, since averages are always most accurate
questions.explain: One $4 million sale spread across ten houses lifts the mean well above what nine buyers actually paid, so the median describes the street better. The trap is treating the mean as automatically the most accurate.

questions.question: Jasmine's five quiz scores are 82, 85, 88, 90, and 95, giving a mean of 88 and a median of 88. She then gets 20 on a quiz she was sick for, making six scores in all. Which measure changes less, and why?
options: The mean; it falls 1.5 while the median falls about 11
The median; both fall the same since 20 is in both
The median; it falls 1.5 and the mean falls about 11
The mean; it must be used since it counts all scores
questions.explain: With six scores the median is the average of 85 and 88, which is 86.5, only 1.5 lower, while the mean drops from 88 to about 76.7. The trap is thinking the low score drags the middle value down as hard as it drags the total.

questions.question: Set A is 12, 14, 15, 16, 18. Set B is 12, 14, 15, 16, 78. In which set does the mean give a better picture of a typical value, and why?
options: Both, since the mean is always the best measure
Set B, since its mean uses the large value 78
Set B, since 78 changes B's median the most
Set A, since no value sits far from the rest
questions.explain: The mean describes data well only when the values cluster; in Set B the 78 pulls the mean to 27, above four of the five values. The trap is judging the mean by how much data it uses instead of by how spread out that data is.

questions.question: At a Burnaby swim meet, six swimmers finish the 50 m race in 34.2 s, 35.0 s, 35.4 s, 36.1 s, 36.3 s, and 58.7 s, because one swimmer stopped to fix her goggles. The mean of the six times is 39.3 s and the median is 35.8 s. The coach must report one number as the team's typical time. What should the coach do?
options: Report 35.8 s, the median; 58.7 s inflates the mean
Report 58.7 s, the slowest, since it counts as well
Report 39.3 s, the mean, because it counts every swim
Report 39.3 s, since 58.7 s shifts the median most
questions.explain: The 58.7 s swim adds over 22 extra seconds to the total, pushing the mean above five of the six times, while the median stays between the middle two swims. The trap is reporting the mean because it uses every time, even when one time is not typical.

questions.question: Owen records what he spends on lunch each school day: $4, $5, $5, $6, and $35, because on Friday he bought lunch for his whole soccer team. He tells his mom that his typical daily lunch cost is $11. What went wrong with his claim?
options: He used the median, which the $35 lunch raised
He used the mean, and the $35 day pulled it up
Nothing is wrong; the mean is always the best one
He added wrong; the five days average to $10
questions.explain: His $55 total divided by 5 days gives a mean of $11, but $35 of that came from one team lunch, so $11 is more than he spent on four of the five days; the median, $5, is typical. The trap is trusting the mean when one value is far from the rest.

questions.question: Seven classes at a Kelowna school donate cans to a food drive: 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, and 90 cans, where the class with 90 also ran a bottle drive. The principal wants one number showing what a typical class donated. Which choice reports the right number with the right reason?
options: Use the mean, 26; it is the fairest share per class
Use the mean, 26; the 90 raised the median to 26
Use the median, 15; the 90 lifts the mean to 26
Use the median, 26; the 90 moved the median most
questions.explain: Order the seven values and the middle one is 15, but the total of 180 divided by 7 gives about 26, more than six of the seven classes donated. The trap is thinking the 90 dragged the median upward, when it only stretched the mean.

questions.question: A Grade 8 class tests how many hours phone batteries last. For the first five phones the times are 9, 10, 10, 11, and 12 hours, so the mean is 10.4 h and the median is 10 h. They then add a sixth, faulty phone that lasted only 2 hours. Which statement about the six phones is correct?
options: The median fell to 6 h; the mean hardly moved at all
The median fell to 9 h while the mean stayed 10.4 h
Both fell to 9 h, since every value counts in each
The mean fell to 9 h but the median stayed 10 h
questions.explain: The new total is 54 over 6 phones, so the mean drops to 9 h, while the two middle values are still 10 and 10, keeping the median at 10 h. The trap is expecting the low outlier to pull the median down too.
